sections.html:
Most of Summerville lies in Dorchester County, and smaller pieces reach into Berkeley and Charleston counties. The 2020 census put the population at 50,915, seventh among South Carolina cities. The town spreads over about 22.7 square miles, only 43 feet above sea level.

Your house's county settles three practical matters: who mails the tax bill, which school district serves you and which register of deeds files the deed. Dorchester County covers most addresses. If yours is near an edge, look at your last tax bill to confirm.

Summerville has protected its trees since an early law in 1847, and the town seal still reads "Sacra Pinus Esto," or the pine is sacred. The Town's rules today:

Tree sizeWhat the Town requires
8 inches or more across at breast height, any species, including dead treesA removal permit
16 inches or moreApproval from the Tree Protection Board
Application fee$10, non-refundable, paid online through the Citizen Serve portal
Removal tied to new constructionSubmitted with the building permit

Removal is typically approved for trees that are dead, diseased, dying or a safety hazard. Do not cut first and ask later. The permit rule applies whether or not the house is for sale. Town Hall can be reached at 843-871-6000.

The Town also issues building permits, stormwater permits and a home occupation special use permit for running a business out of a house. Most applications go in online through Citizen Serve. Town Hall is at 200 South Main Street, 843-871-6000.

When an earlier owner added a room, deck or garage, collect whatever permit records you have before the buyer's attorney asks. Gaps in the paperwork can slow a conventional sale. A cash buyer may be more willing to accept the house as it stands, provided the price reflects the risk.

Interstate 26 has four exits in town: Jedburg Road, Nexton Parkway, US 17A and College Park Road. US 78 runs about 24 miles to downtown Charleston, and US 176, SC 165, SC 642 and SC 61 also pass through.

Public school students in the Dorchester County portion attend Dorchester School District Two, which runs Summerville High, Ashley Ridge High and Fort Dorchester High. Berkeley County and Charleston County districts serve their portions of the town.

With about 108 rainy days a year and a low elevation, Summerville houses get a hard look at drainage, crawlspace moisture and roof condition during inspections. Unsure whether your lot sits in a mapped flood area? Ask the Town or county before listing, since a buyer's lender and insurer will care about the answer.

sections.h2: Dorchester County property tax after a sale
sections.html: After a sale, Dorchester County sets the house at market value. Most transfers count as assessable transfers of interest and are valued as of December 31 of the sale year. Owners who live in the house may qualify for the 4 percent legal residence rate through the Assessor's Office in St. George or Summerville, and ownership, address or use changes must be reported within six months.

sections.h2: Due dates, penalties and the Treasurer
sections.html:
• Dorchester bills fall due January 15. The Treasurer's Office takes payment of current property taxes, vehicle taxes and registration fees.
  • State law adds penalties of 3, 7 and 5 percent in stages after the due date.
  • Mobile homes must be registered within 15 days of purchase or relocation, with fines up to $200.

Call or email the Treasurer at Treasurer@DorchesterCountySC.gov for the current-year schedule and for a payoff figure before closing.

Before the contract is signed, a seller typically hands the buyer a written condition statement. It touches structure, plumbing, electrical and heating systems, termite damage that was never repaired and environmental hazards. You may report real knowledge or make no representation. Estate sales by a fiduciary are among the exempt transfers.

The same statute permits as-is sales, though the statement is still owed unless the sale is exempt. Price normally adjusts for repairs the buyer takes on.

When the buyer pays cash, no loan stands between you and closing, so no lender appraisal holds the date. A closing attorney still searches the title, clears liens and records the deed. Put any offer next to what repairs, carrying costs and time on the market would cost you, and insist on having it in writing.

Begin by describing the house: which county it is in, any open permits and whether trees or drainage have caused trouble. We look it over in its present state and write up any offer. You then pick the closing date.

A cash purchase also spares you showings and the back and forth of repair requests. For many owners that saved effort is as valuable as the speed.

sections.h2: Selling when trees or drainage are the issue
sections.html:
A big dead tree beside the house, or water pooling against the foundation, can sour a buyer on the whole property. Because the Town requires a permit for removing a tree of 8 inches or more across, including a dead one, start that process early if a tree needs to come down.

If you would rather not deal with it before selling, say so up front. A cash buyer can account for the tree, the drainage or a soft crawlspace in the price, and you avoid weeks of waiting on approvals and contractors.

Closing day is mostly signatures: the deed and the settlement statement. Your attorney verifies the title, settles the mortgage and any taxes owed out of your proceeds and files the deed in the proper county. Hold on to a copy of every page.

If a small piece of your property is in Berkeley or Charleston County, mention it at the start so the attorney records in the correct place. Afterward, give the county your new mailing address so later notices reach you, and end your homeowner policy only once the sale is recorded. Doing it in that order avoids a gap in coverage.

Find your latest tax bill from Dorchester, Berkeley or Charleston County, a mortgage payoff figure and any permit records for additions. A house held through an estate needs the papers that show who may sign. Having them ready keeps the closing date from slipping.

Ask the Treasurer for a current balance before closing. Unpaid taxes come out of the proceeds, and knowing the amount ahead of time avoids a last-minute change to what you walk away with.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to remove a tree before selling in Summerville?
faqs.a: Yes, for most larger trees. The Town requires a permit for any tree 8 inches or more in diameter at breast height, including dead ones, and trees 16 inches or more need Tree Protection Board approval. The application fee is $10.

faqs.q: Which county bills property tax on a Summerville house?
faqs.a: Dorchester County, for most addresses. Small parts of town are in Berkeley and Charleston counties, so your last tax bill is the way to confirm yours.

faqs.q: What happens to my Dorchester County property tax value after I sell?
faqs.a: Typically the sale is an assessable transfer of interest, which resets the new owner's value to market as of December 31 of that year. A buyer who will live there can apply for the 4 percent legal residence rate.

faqs.q: When are Summerville property taxes due?
faqs.a: Dorchester County bills are due January 15, with penalties starting afterward under state law.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Summerville house as-is?
faqs.a: Yes, as-is sales are allowed in South Carolina. You still owe the disclosure statement unless your sale is exempt, and buyers usually adjust their price for repairs.
